results.summary: Lizard Mountain's page now starts and ends at Cascade Pass, because the Suiattle River Road to the southern Downey Creek trailhead is closed until at least January 2028.
results.evidence: The Forest Service closure alert confirms the Suiattle River Road is closed at milepost 4 from April 2, 2026 to January 1, 2028, and the Downey Creek trail page says the trailhead is cut off by washouts. A guide service's 2026 notice replaces its traverse with an out-and-back from Cascade Pass or a South Cascade River exit. An independent 2024 out-and-back from Cascade Pass reached White Rock Lakes via the Le Conte Glacier, around Sentinel Peak, across the South Cascade Glacier and over Lizard Col, and scrambled Lizard by the south ridge, descending the west ridge - so the north-side text crossing the South Cascade Glacier is correct; the mislabel was only on the south side (Itswoot Ridge to Lizard Col goes via Spire Col and the Dana Glacier), fixed in the closed southern variant. Cascade Pass trailhead: 48.4754,-121.0751, no parking fee, 3.7 mi/1,800 ft to the 5,392 ft pass. Summit height: one peak list gives 7,420 ft, others 7,400-7,408 ft; nothing independent gives 7,399, so the row's own 7,420 (high_point_ft, pitch_detail) is applied everywhere. Totals (35 mi, 11,200 ft gain) are the row's own per-day figures mirrored for the return; the itinerary grows to 7 days. The itinerary's 'a real trip report calls it' citation was reworded.

ops.expect: Lizard Mountain has no dedicated trailhead — the accepted approach follows the southern leg of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor out of the Downey Creek Trailhead (~1,450 ft) on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) east of Darrington. Take Downey Creek Trail #768, which enters Glacier Peak Wilderness within the first half-mile and climbs gently through old-growth forest, crossing several tributary creeks (can run high in early season) for about 6.6 miles to the Bachelor Creek Trail junction near 2,400 ft. Turn onto the Bachelor Creek climbers' path — unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown (expect to step over or crawl under numerous downed trees) plus a brushy alder/slide-alder band around 3,800–4,400 ft that becomes a real bushwhack when snow hasn't flattened it. The trail fords Bachelor Creek itself, which flows fast and cold with snowmelt in early-mid summer — scout for a log crossing or plan on wet feet. Above treeline the trail breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake (~5,340 ft), a reliable water source and common first camp. From Cub Lake, climb a steep, often snow-covered pitch onto Itswoot Ridge (~6,350 ft), another established camp with tarn water. Beyond Itswoot Ridge the route goes cross-country (boot path in season) toward and across South Cascade Glacier — a real glacier with crevasse hazard, especially late-season when snow bridges have opened up; rope travel is prudent unless the glacier is fully consolidated. This crossing tops out at Lizard Col (~6,798 ft), the broad notch on Lizard Mountain's south ridge overlooking White Rock Lakes to the southwest. Trailhead to Lizard Col is roughly 14–15 miles one-way with on the order of 5,000+ ft of net gain (more once the undulating up-and-over-Itswoot-Ridge terrain is counted), so almost everyone treats this as a 2–3 day round trip rather than a day climb — matching the ~29-mile (46.67 km) round-trip distance. From the col, the South Route gains Lizard Mountain's south ridge directly to the summit, a straightforward but loose Class 2 scramble of roughly 600 vertical feet, staying near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks.
ops.value: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own. It is climbed from a camp at White Rock Lakes, which parties reach from the north over the first half of the Ptarmigan Traverse and leave the same way. Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of the Cascade River Road, 23 miles from Marblemount. The maintained trail switchbacks about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft up to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last built tread of the trip. From the pass a climbers' path traverses south-southeast across the flank of Mixup Peak to the Cache Glacier; rope up for the glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then drop to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), the usual first camp. Beyond the lake the Red Ledge crosses the cliff band, and a roped crossing of the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the gap beside Spider Mountain and down to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft). From there climb onto the Le Conte Glacier, work around Sentinel Peak, cross the broad South Cascade Glacier and top out at Lizard Col (~6,800 ft) on Lizard's south ridge, then descend to White Rock Lakes (~6,200 ft). From camp, regain the col and follow the south ridge roughly 600 vertical feet to the summit, a short but loose Class 2-3 scramble; stay near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks. Most parties take three days to reach White Rock Lakes, and the whole outing is about 35 miles round trip with some 11,000 ft of cumulative gain. The southern approach from the Downey Creek Trailhead is not usable at present: the Suiattle River Road is closed at milepost 4 until at least January 2028, and washouts cut off the trailhead.

ops.expect: Reverse the Class 3 scramble back down to Lizard Pass and the White Rock Lakes camp — there is no separate descent trail. From camp, retrace the way you came in: south past Spire Col and Cub Lake, then down Bachelor Creek to the Downey Creek trail and the trailhead. Parties who are instead walking the full Ptarmigan Traverse pick Lizard up mid-route and carry on to the other end, finishing at Cascade Pass rather than Downey Creek — that is a shuttle trip and a different outing from the approach described here.
ops.value: Reverse the Class 3 scramble to Lizard Col and drop back to the White Rock Lakes camp; there is no separate descent trail, though the west ridge is a common way back down to the col. From camp, retrace the way in: over Lizard Col and across the South Cascade and Le Conte Glaciers to Yang Yang Lakes, over the Middle Cascade Glacier and along the Red Ledge to Kool-Aid Lake, then up to Cache Col and down to Cascade Pass and the trailhead. Plan on three days from camp back to the car. The old southern exit over Spire Col and down Bachelor Creek to the Downey Creek Trailhead is cut off while the Suiattle River Road is closed.

ops.expect: Reverse the south ridge scramble from the summit back down to Lizard Col — this is Class 2 the whole way with no rappelling required on the peak itself (rappels: 0). From the col, retrace the approach: back across South Cascade Glacier (same crevasse caution as the ascent) to Itswoot Ridge, down the steep pitch to Cub Lake, back down the loose, blowdown-choked Bachelor Creek climbers' path (re-fording Bachelor Creek), and out Downey Creek Trail #768 to the trailhead — the same 14–15 miles and net elevation loss as the approach. Because of the length, most parties descend only as far as camp at Itswoot Ridge or Cub Lake on summit day and walk out to the trailhead the following day. There is no shorter or technical alternate descent documented for this route; it is a walk/scramble-off, not a rappel route.
ops.value: Reverse the south ridge from the summit to Lizard Col. It is loose Class 2 the whole way and needs no rappels; many parties use the west ridge as an alternative way back down to the col. From the col, drop to camp at White Rock Lakes, then retrace the approach north: across the South Cascade Glacier and around Sentinel Peak on the Le Conte Glacier to Yang Yang Lakes, over the Middle Cascade Glacier and along the Red Ledge to Kool-Aid Lake, then up to Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier and across to Cascade Pass, and down the trail to the Cascade River Road. The glaciers carry the same crevasse hazard on the way out as on the way in, and most parties take three days from White Rock Lakes back to the car.

expect.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
expect.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
expect.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
the Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
loose blocks on the summit ridge itself
expect.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

expect.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek
expect.notes: The other end of the same corridor, and the shorter way if Lizard is the objective rather than the traverse. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown — expect to step over and crawl under a great deal of it — with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt; scout for a log rather than committing to a wet crossing. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge, another established camp with tarn water, and from there the route goes cross-country across the South Cascade Glacier to top out at the col on Lizard's south ridge.
expect.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
hazards: sustained blowdown and slide-alder bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
the Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
crevasse hazard on the South Cascade Glacier, worst late season once snow bridges have opened
multi-day evacuation distance with no cell coverage
loose blocks near the summit crest

expect.status: Suiattle River Road is closed to motor vehicles at milepost 4 (washout, closure order April 2, 2026 - January 1, 2028); the Downey Creek trailhead beyond it is currently cut off by multiple washouts.
expect.driveNote: Neither road reaches Lizard Mountain directly -- both lead only to trailheads that begin the multi-day Ptarmigan Traverse.
expect.seasonalGate: Cascade River Road gates at Eldorado (MP 20) over winter and typically reopens to the Cascade Pass trailhead by late June or July.

value.name: Cascade River Road
value.status: The Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass Trailhead is the only usable access. The Suiattle River Road, the old southern access to Downey Creek, is closed to motor vehicles at milepost 4 (closure order April 2, 2026 - January 1, 2028).
value.driveNote: From SR 20 at Marblemount, the Cascade River Road runs about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead; the peak is three days of off-trail glacier travel beyond it.
value.seasonalGate: Cascade River Road gates at Eldorado (MP 20) over winter and typically reopens to the Cascade Pass trailhead by late June or July.

ops.expect: The approach crosses South Cascade Glacier, a real glacier with crevasse hazard that increases late season as snow bridges open - rope travel is prudent unless the glacier is fully consolidated; the summit ridge scramble itself is not glaciated.
ops.value: The approach crosses four glaciers each way (Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade), with crevasse hazard that increases late season as snow bridges open; rope travel is prudent on all of them. The summit ridge scramble itself is not glaciated.

results.resolution: keep_as_A: page stays on the Hannegan Pass approach; itinerary rebuilt as a 5-day Hannegan trip camping near Brush Creek (Bear Creek camp closed), timing and totals recomputed, Chilliwack-side hours removed from the approach and camp waypoint, Chilliwack Lake variant kept as secondary with a border caution
results.summary: The North Buttress day plan now starts at Hannegan Pass like the rest of the page, as a 5-day trip of about 45 miles and 12,000 ft, instead of the 3-day Chilliwack Lake (Canada) trip it used to describe.
results.evidence: The Park Service trail-conditions page confirms the Chilliwack River Trail is cleared to Bear Creek camp and that Bear Creek camp is closed for 2021 fire damage; its Copper Ridge page puts Boundary Camp 5 mi from the Hannegan trailhead and the Brush Creek junction 7 mi beyond, i.e. about 12 mi in. The route database gives ~17 mi from Hannegan to Bear Creek, and the Chilliwack Lake start as ~9 mi/4,500 ft/9 h to the 6,480 ft saddle, with the tread overgrown past the border at ~1.7 mi. An independent 5-day Hannegan trip to Bear camped at Brush Creek the first night and totalled ~36 mi and 12,500 ft (by a shorter west-slope line from the Copper Ridge junction), confirming 4-5 days and ~12,000 ft. A cross-border hiking article says the Chilliwack River Trail can no longer be walked through continuously. Nothing found contradicts building the page on Hannegan. Per-day figures: TH 3,100 ft, Hannegan Pass 5,066 ft, Brush Creek ~12 mi in, Bear Creek 2,300 ft at ~17 mi, saddle camp 6,480 ft at ~21 mi (the row's own waypoints); summit day unchanged.

expect.cal: Best climbed July-September once the Chilliwack River Trail and approach gullies are snow-free; the US-side trailhead is reached via Hannegan Pass or Chilliwack Lake Road (partly in BC), so check current border-crossing/trail-access conditions before going.

days.note: From the Chilliwack Lake trailhead, follow the Chilliwack River Trail roughly 6 miles (about 5 hours) to Bear Creek Camp at 2,300'. Just past Bear Creek, leave the trail and climb steep timber and huckleberry slopes on the unmarked 'Bear Creek High Route' past Ruta Lake to meadows on the NW ridge, then traverse below Points 6592 and 6822 to a good camping saddle at 6,480'.

ops.find: All told this is roughly 9-9.5 hours and 4,500+ ft of gain from the trailhead to camp, so most parties split it over two days. A shorter but more logistically complex alternative exists via Chilliwack Lake Road in BC (~9 miles to camp) but requires a border crossing/passport and follows an overgrown, unmaintained tread after the first 1.7 miles — most US-based parties use the Hannegan approach instead.
ops.replace: All told this is roughly 21 miles and about 6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead to camp, which most parties split over two days, camping on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek because the Bear Creek camp has been closed since the 2021 fire. A much shorter line (~9 miles to camp) starts from Chilliwack Lake Road in BC, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry and follows an overgrown, unmaintained tread after the first 1.7 miles; the Hannegan approach is the one to plan on.

results.resolution: keep_as_A: kept as its own climb on the Hannegan Pass approach; gain/loss/distance set to the same Hannegan round-trip totals as the sister North Buttress rebuild (11,950 ft, 72.4 km), approach time 18 h, approach prose and itinerary text rewritten, stale '2026' fire-closure claims corrected, Chilliwack Lake variant given a border caution
results.summary: The Direct North Buttress stays a separate climb, and its distance and elevation totals now describe the long Hannegan Pass approach its trailhead actually uses rather than the short Canadian start.
results.evidence: The route database lists the Direct North Buttress (Kearney-Knight 1980) as a 21-pitch 5.10- line starting from the toe of the buttress, distinct from the 1967 North Buttress, which walks past the toe on the neve to a slab-and-corner start, so no merge. The Park Service fire-closure page (updated September 14, 2026) lists no 2026 fire and no closure of the Chilliwack River Trail, and the trail-conditions page says the trail is cleared to Bear Creek camp, which is closed for 2021 fire damage; the Hannegan-trailhead closure order came from the 2022 Chilliwack Complex, so the row's '2026' closure claims were wrong. Distance/gain use the sister row's Hannegan figures (Brush Creek ~12 mi in per the Park Service mileages, Bear Creek ~17 mi, saddle camp ~21 mi; a documented 5-day Hannegan trip to Bear ran ~36 mi and 12,500 ft). The bivy list no longer contains an Ouzel Lake/Depot Creek camp, so nothing to drop.

ops.find: The summit goes via the west ridge and upper north ridge (Class 4-5 scrambling) or the Northwest Ridge, the most commonly cited standard route. Round trips typically run 4-6 days with 30+ miles and well over 10,000 ft of gain.
ops.replace: From camp the Direct is reached by dropping to the glacier remnant below the wall and tying in where the toe of the buttress meets the snow; the descent from the summit returns to the same camp. The trailhead-to-camp leg is roughly 21 miles and 6,500 ft of gain, usually split over two days with a night on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek, because the camp at the Bear Creek confluence has been closed since the 2021 fire. Round trips typically run 5-6 days, about 45 miles and roughly 12,000 ft of gain.

ops.expect: Day 1: approach to saddle camp (~6,480 ft). Days 2-3: climb the 21-pitch buttress (historically done in about 2.5 days with a bivy), then descend to camp. Day 4: hike out.

Days 3-4: climb the 21-pitch buttress (historically done in about 2.5 days with a bivy), then descend to camp. Days 5-6: hike back out over Hannegan Pass, about 21 miles.

results.resolution: keep_as_A: kept as the West Ridge (Beckey Route) from Depot Creek; itinerary and timing rebuilt as a 4-day Depot Creek trip (Ouzel Lake, Redoubt Glacier saddle camp, summit day via the Col of the Wild, out), gain/loss 7,200 ft, distance 33.2 km (20.6 mi, matching the row's waypoints), road block rewritten for Chilliwack Lake Road and the Depot Creek spur
results.summary: The Hard Mox West Ridge page's day plan now follows the Depot Creek approach the rest of the page describes, replacing a Ross Lake boat-and-Perry-Creek plan that belongs to a different trip.
results.evidence: The route database places this 3-pitch 5.5 route above a 7,200 ft camp at the head of Depot Creek, reached from Canada. An independent Depot Creek trip for both Mox peaks went Depot Creek parking (2,350 ft) to Ouzel Lake (~9 mi incl. road, 3,550 ft, ~9 h), Ouzel Lake to the Redoubt Glacier saddle (7,150 ft; 3.2 mi, 1,550 ft), then Hard Mox via the Col of the Wild and the Gendarme notch, totalling ~24 mi and 11,200 ft over several days including Easy Mox; the Park Service's own Depot Creek condition post describes the border-to-Ouzel-Lake path and the falls handlines. A hiking report describes the Depot Creek spur as a rough, overgrown 4x4 road off Chilliwack Lake Road just before a gated bridge over Depot Creek. No account of this climb uses a Ross Lake water taxi or a Perry Creek bivy, and the Park Service fire-closure page lists Perry Creek camp and the Little Beaver trail beyond Little Beaver camp as closed. Per-day mileages follow the row's own waypoint chain (10.3 mi to the summit); the specific 'locked gate about 0.9 mi up' in the recommendation could not be confirmed, so it was not written.

expect.cal: The Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver only runs 8 AM-5 PM and must be booked in advance; a North Cascades NP backcountry permit is required for the overnight bivy.

A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit covers the camps at Ouzel Lake and the Redoubt Glacier saddle. Best from mid-July into September, once the slabs beside Depot Creek Falls are free of snow.

results.resolution: keep_as_A with the 2-day plan kept: day 1 rewritten as the short walk from the road, the river crossing and the couloir climb to a bivy at the C-J col (its existing 6 h / 3 mi / 3,200 ft already fit that), day 2 rewritten to start from the col bivy on the East Ridge and descend by the couloir only if firm, else Doug's Direct; totals and hours unchanged
results.summary: The day plan keeps its night at the Cascade-Johannesburg col, because the one-day reports behind the recommendation were ski descents of the couloir that never went to the summit; only the wrong 'hike the Cascade Pass trail' description and the schedule were fixed.
results.evidence: Both reports cited for a one-day trip are ski outings that climbed the couloir only to the col and skied back down (one on January 24, 2025); neither climbed the East Ridge to Johannesburg's summit, so they do not show the summit climb is a day trip. They do confirm the couloir apron is about 20 minutes and under a mile from the road via a river crossing, and that the couloir is 3,000+ ft to the col, so day 1's 'hike the Cascade Pass trail' wording was wrong while its figures (3 mi, 3,200 ft, 6 h) fit a climb of the couloir to the col. East Ridge summit accounts describe 2-3 day trips with camps at or just below the C-J col (a heather bench near 6,200 ft; a col bivy with easy snow access), and the row's own bivy list names the C-J col bivy as where most parties sleep. Day 2's gain (1,400 ft) and loss (4,600 ft) likewise match col-to-summit and summit-to-car. The old schedule started day 2 up the couloir from the bivy, contradicting a col bivy, and cited 'trip reports'; both fixed.

ops.expect: Hike the Cascade Pass trail then cut cross-country toward Cascade-Johannesburg col, gaining the flanks below the couloir. Most parties reach a flat bivy spot near the col with time to rest before an alpine-start next morning.
ops.value: Walk a short way back down the road from the Cascade Pass trailhead, drop through brush into the valley and cross the Cascade River, then cross the moraine to the apron of the couloir at about 3,300 ft, roughly twenty minutes from the road. Start early while the snow is firm and climb about 3,000 ft of snow in the couloir with overnight gear to the bivy at the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

ops.expect: An alpine-start ascent of the snow couloir onto the ridge crest, then sustained, loose, exposed 3rd-5th class climbing along the East Ridge to the true summit. The whole route is then downclimbed/rappelled and the couloir descended before it softens, followed by the long hike out — real parties report finishing well after dark.
ops.value: An alpine start from the col bivy onto the East Ridge, then sustained, loose, exposed 3rd-5th class climbing along the ridge to the true summit. The ridge is downclimbed and short-rappelled back to the col, and the party then descends to the trailhead: down the couloir only if it has stayed firm, otherwise by the longer Doug's Direct traverse to Cascade Pass. Most parties finish well after dark.

ops.find: roughly 6 hours to a bivy near the C-J col, then a brutal 18-20+ hour summit day climbing the couloir and East Ridge and reversing the entire route back to the trailhead.
ops.replace: roughly 6 hours up the couloir to a bivy at the C-J col, then a brutal 18-20+ hour summit day on the East Ridge and back down to the trailhead.

ops.expect: Hike the Cascade Pass trail then cut cross-country toward Cascade-Johannesburg col, gaining the flanks below the couloir. Most parties reach a flat bivy spot near the col with time…
ops.value: Walk a short way back down the road from the Cascade Pass trailhead, drop through brush into the valley and cross the Cascade River, then cross the moraine to the apron of the couloir at about 3,300 ft, roughly twenty minutes from the road. Start early while the snow is firm and climb about 3,000 ft of snow in the couloir with overnight gear to the bivy at the Cascade-Johannesburg col.

ops.find: An alpine-start ascent of the snow couloir onto the ridge crest, then
ops.replace: An alpine start from the col bivy onto the East Ridge, then

ops.value: 3:00 AM from the C-J col bivy
